title: Remedies for the passions and the need for stillness and struggle
english: Fasting cuts away lack of self-control in food, and self-control with prayer takes away the licentiousness of fornication. Poverty restrains love of money, the mother of idolatry, and hope in God cuts away bodily worry. Reading the words of God restrains a wandering mind, as does keeping vigil with prayer. Patience and psalmody calm the assault of anger. Endurance and tears hold listlessness in check, and hatred of pleasures silences worldly grief. Humility gains hospitality, and turning away from love of power and preeminence, while humility without measure stops pride—that ancient evil, abominable in the sight of the Lord, which God himself opposes—the humility that says, “I am earth and ashes” (Genesis 18:27), and again, “Unless the Lord builds the house, the builder has labored in vain” (Psalm 127:1), and strives to guard it. Just as muddied water cannot become clear unless it stays still, so a monk cannot know his own state without stillness. Just as an athlete cannot be crowned without wrestling, so no one can become a Christian without struggles.
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.
orientation: Evagrius opens the work by listing each passion and its remedy, then states that a monk's state cannot be known without stillness and that one cannot become a Christian without struggles.
